title: The Art of Disagreement
author: Hallett, Ian
summary: Ian Hallett opens with the contested 2025 STAAR Surgical board vote — where a unanimous board backed a $1.5 billion sale, the company's largest shareholder publicly opposed it, and shareholders ultimately rejected a 59% premium — then tracked the outcome: within months the business was posting record-high quarterly revenues the board had declared impossible as a standalone company. Hallett uses this case to make a counterintuitive claim: that disagreement in organizations is not a process for finding the right answer but a process for making a properly tested decision — and that the two are not the same thing. When capable people reason from the same evidence to opposite conclusions, the disagreement is a property of the decision's inherent uncertainty, not a failure by either party. Three common failures corrupt this: leaders judge the quality of the argument by its eventual outcome (unavailable information); they mistake unanimity for alignment (boards that never split have often just learned dissent is unwelcome); and they let disagreement stay private where it carries all the cost of division without any of the benefit. Hallett closes with four implementable mechanisms — name both positions before debating, assign the counter-case to someone credible, ask what would have to be true, and record the reasoning not just the decision — arguing that a well-run disagreement is actually faster than a falsely unanimous one because it is bounded, tested, and unlikely to be relitigated.
points: Hallett's central reframe is that disagreement is not a search for the right answer but a mechanism for making a properly tested decision — the STAAR case proves that both sides can be entirely defensible at the moment of decision, because the facts that would settle the argument have not yet occurred.

Treating the outcome as the verdict on the argument is the most seductive and common error in organizational disagreement: it grades the quality of the process using information nobody had when the argument took place, and systematically rewards whoever happened to be on the winning side of an inherently uncertain call.

A board that always votes unanimously is not proof of alignment — it may simply have learned that dissent is unwelcome, and that lesson's cost is invisible until something goes badly wrong; STAAR's decision to publicly disclose its split vote was the signal that the argument had been real.

The single most useful question in a contested decision is 'What would have to be true?' — because it moves the argument from opinion to evidence, forces each side to state its conditions, and clarifies which conditions can actually be tested now versus which represent genuine irreducible uncertainty.

Recording the reasoning behind a decision — not just the outcome, but the strongest counter-argument and what you expect to see if you are wrong — is described as 'the closest thing to a superpower available to a leadership team' because it prevents post-hoc history rewriting and enables honest review of judgment.
quotes: And here is what almost every leader gets wrong about disagreement. You were taught to treat it as a process for finding the right answer. In the decisions that matter most, there is often no single right answer available at the moment you must decide, and pretending otherwise is how organisations talk themselves into false confidence.

When two capable, well-informed people reach opposite conclusions from the same evidence, it is usually because the thing itself is uncertain, not because one of them has reasoned badly. The disagreement is a property of the decision, not a defect in the person you are disagreeing with.

If you believe the argument should produce truth, then whoever fails to persuade you is wrong, or obstructive, or protecting something. That is precisely how the STAAR fight turned personal, with each side eventually questioning the other's motives rather than their reasoning.
A board that always votes unanimously is not necessarily aligned. It may simply have learned that dissent is unwelcome, and the cost of that lesson is invisible until something goes badly wrong.

The most dangerous version of dissent is the kind expressed in corridors and side conversations. It carries all the cost of division and none of the benefit, because the decision never gets tested by it.

A well-run disagreement is fast, because it is bounded. The positions are defined, the counter-case is evaluated, the uncertainty is stated, and then somebody decides. What actually slows organisations down is the objection nobody voiced that surfaces three months later, the executive who never really agreed and withholds effort, or the decision that gets relitigated because it was never properly argued the first time.
